subject: Abigail
note: Evidence for Abigail's Bible figure page. A thin record: one chapter of story (1 Samuel 25) and five mentions in lists (1 Samuel 27:3; 30:5, 18; 2 Samuel 2:2; 3:3; 1 Chronicles 3:1), so a short page: eight moments, no miracles section (none are hers; Nabal's death is the LORD's act and is told among the moments), no death section (Scripture tells nothing of her end, and no later legend of it was found worth printing), no type box (the personality test does not name her), no feasts section (no church keeps a day for her). Every quotation is in abigail.quotes.json and passes verify-quotes.mjs. Bible lines are from the Berean Standard Bible (shared/bsb-berean-standard-bible.txt); the Fathers are from shared/npnf210.txt, npnf211.txt and npnf212.txt. Fetched texts are in design/saints-hub/sources/people/abigail/ (gitignored).

life.text: Nabal of Maon, whose business was in Carmel, was very wealthy (3,000 sheep, 1,000 goats); his wife was Abigail, an intelligent and beautiful woman; he was harsh and evil in his dealings, a Calebite.
life.note: Josephus, Antiquities 6.13.6, calls her 'a woman of a good character, wise and handsome'.

life.text: Carmel is a town in the hill country of Judah, listed with Maon (Joshua 15:55), not Mount Carmel.
life.source: Joshua 15:48, 55 (BSB): 'In the hill country ... Maon, Carmel, Ziph, Juttah'. Jewish Encyclopedia (1906), 'Abigail': 'the town of Carmel in southern Judah'.

life.text: David, in the wilderness, sent ten young men at shearing time; his men had protected Nabal's shepherds; Nabal answered 'Who is David?'; David and about 400 men strapped on swords, 200 stayed with the supplies.
One of Nabal's young men told Abigail; 'They were a wall around us'; 'nobody can speak to him'.
Her gift: 200 loaves, 2 skins of wine, 5 butchered sheep, 5 seahs of roasted grain, 100 clusters of raisins, 200 cakes of figs, loaded on donkeys; she sent her young men ahead and did not tell Nabal.
life.note: The page says 'five measures of roasted grain' in narration for the BSB's 'five seahs'.

life.text: She met David in a mountain ravine, got off the donkey, fell facedown; her plea runs 1 Samuel 25:24-31 (eight verses); David blessed her discernment, accepted the gift and said 'Go home in peace'.
life.note: Her speech is the longest in 1 Samuel 25 (David's are verses 21-22, 32-34 and 35). The page does NOT claim it is the longest speech by a woman in the Bible: Hannah's prayer (1 Samuel 2:1-10) is longer.

life.text: Nabal was feasting and very drunk; she told him nothing until morning; when sober he heard, his heart failed and he became like a stone; about ten days later the LORD struck him dead.
life.source: 1 Samuel 25:36-38 (BSB). Josephus, Antiquities 6.13.8: 'so Nabal survived ten days, and no more, and then died'.

life.text: David sent to ask her to be his wife; she bowed and said 'Here is your servant...'; she went with five maidens; David had also married Ahinoam of Jezreel; Michal had been given to Palti.

She went with David to Achish at Gath; Achish gave David Ziklag; Amalekites burned Ziklag and took the women captive, Abigail and Ahinoam among them; David's men wept and spoke of stoning him; David found strength in the LORD, pursued and recovered everything including his two wives.
She went up with David to Hebron, where he was anointed king over Judah; her son Chileab, David's second son, was born there; 1 Chronicles 3:1 calls him Daniel. This is the Bible's last word on her.
life.source: 2 Samuel 2:1-4; 3:2-3; 1 Chronicles 3:1 (BSB). Josephus, Antiquities 7.1.4: 'the second was Daniel, by his wife Abigail'.
life.note: The Jewish Encyclopedia (1906) adds that Chileab 'appears ... to have died before reaching manhood': an inference, not used.

life.text: Her name: Hebrew Abigayil, probably 'my father is joy'.
life.source: Bible Hub, Strong's Hebrew 26 (Brown-Driver-Briggs: 'my father is joy (?)'; Strong's: 'father (i.e. source) of joy'). Encyclopaedia Britannica (1911), 'Abigail': 'perhaps "father is joy"'.

life.text: A second Abigail in the Bible: David's sister, mother of Amasa, whom Absalom appointed over his army.

said.text: Josephus: 'having received that honor on account of her wise and righteous course of life'.
said.source: Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews, book 6, chapter 13, section 8, tr. William Whiston (Project Gutenberg 2848).

said.text: Ambrose: David blessed her who intervened, because he was restrained from revenge.
said.source: Ambrose, On the Duties of the Clergy, Book 1, chapter 21 (section 94), NPNF 2/10.

said.text: Cassian's Abba Joseph: when Abigail interceded, David gave up his threats and preferred to be a breaker of his word rather than keep his oath cruelly.
said.source: John Cassian, Conferences 17 (the second conference of Abbot Joseph), chapter 25, NPNF 2/11.

said.text: Gregory the Great: Abigail laudably kept silence while Nabal was drunk and as laudably told him when sober.
said.source: Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule, Part III, chapter 16 (Admonition 17, the meek and the passionate), NPNF 2/12.
said.note: shared/npnf212.txt. The same Book III the site's Christian Personality Test is built on.

said.text: The Haggadah regards Abigail as one of the most remarkable women in Jewish history; one of the four great beauties with Sarah, Rahab and Esther (Megillah 15a); a prophetess.
said.note: File: people/abigail/je-abigail-1906.txt. The JE also reports a rabbinic charge of 'coquetry' over 'remember your servant': left off as a slight that needs more room than the page has to present fairly.

said.text: The Talmud's seven prophetesses: Sarah, Miriam, Deborah, Hannah, Abigail, Huldah and Esther.
said.source: Babylonian Talmud, Megillah 14a (Sefaria, William Davidson edition, read for the fact only; not quoted).
said.note: File: people/abigail/sefaria-megillah-14a.txt (CC BY-NC translation: never quoted on the page).

tidbits.text: 'abigail' = a lady's maid; Merriam-Webster: from Abigail, servant in The Scornful Lady by Beaumont and Fletcher, first known use 1616; Britannica 1911: from the biblical Abigail, self-styled 'handmaid', cf. the Scornful Lady.
tidbits.source: Merriam-Webster, 'abigail'; Encyclopaedia Britannica (1911), vol. 1, 'Abigail' (Wikisource page 93); Webster's 1913: 'A lady's waiting-maid'.
tidbits.note: Files: mw-abigail.txt, eb1911-abigail-page93.txt, w1913.txt. Both sides of the word's origin are given.

tidbits.text: Her son's names: Chileab (Hebrew, 2 Samuel 3:3), Daluyah (Septuagint), Daniel (1 Chronicles 3:1).
tidbits.note: Cut from the page to keep the numbers column level with the facts; the facts and the circle already give Chileab and Daniel.

tidbits.text: Maarten van Heemskerck's Beatitudes series (engraved by Harmen Jansz Muller, published by Karel Collaert, 1564 to 1568): 'Blessed are the peacemakers' is shown by Abigail kneeling before David, with Matthew 5:9 in Latin.
tidbits.source: Rijksmuseum RP-P-1907-1995 and RP-P-1982-18, as recorded on their Commons file pages.

tidbits.text: Jewish headstones most often end with the abbreviation of 'May his soul be bound in the bundle of life', a paraphrase of 1 Samuel 25:29.
tidbits.source: Pealim, 'The definitive guide to reading Hebrew headstones'. The Jewish Encyclopedia (1906), 'Tombstones', prints Elijah Levita's epitaph of 1549 ending 'his soul is bound up in the bundle of life'.
tidbits.note: Files: pealim-headstones.txt, je-tombstones-1906.txt. Printed as the context line of her feature quotation.

calendar.text: No church keeps a feast day for her.
calendar.source: Searched for Abigail: shared/martyrology-1916.txt, calendarium-romanum-1969-ocr.txt, usccb-2026cal.txt, cofe-calendar.txt, lff2022.txt, lsb-calendar.txt, elca-churchyear.txt, wikipedia-coptic-calendar.txt (no hits); OCA lives search for 'ABIGAIL' returns no Abigail (people/abigail/oca-search-abigail.txt).
calendar.note: CatholicSaints.Info lists 'Abigail the Matriarch' with '1 September': it names no calendar that keeps it, so it is not used. An icon seller (Damascene Gallery) says she is honoured on the Sunday of the Forefathers; the OCA's Forefathers page does not name her, so it is not used.

could_not_verify: The current (2004) Roman Martyrology was not on disk: the page's Catholic note names the 1916 edition only. No Abigail was found in the 1916 edition, the 1969 Calendarium or the USCCB 2026 calendar.
The Greek synaxarion and the Russian menologion were not searched; only the OCA's lives were. The page says 'No day of her own' for the Orthodox.
Where Molinari's painting hangs today: Commons and Wikidata name no collection.
A later legend of her death or burial (a 'Tomb of the Matriarchs' in Tiberias appears in a Commons category): not researched, so no death section and no legend.

checked: Numbers and details against the BSB: about 400 men with David and 200 with the supplies (1 Samuel 25:13); the gift list (25:18); 3,000 sheep and 1,000 goats; about ten days; five maidens; the Ziklag raid and 'including his two wives' (30:18).

Attributions: Josephus, Antiquities 6.13; Ambrose, On the Duties of the Clergy, Book 1, chapter 21 (heading confirmed in npnf210); Gregory, Pastoral Rule III.16 (the passage is on correcting the passionate once their anger has passed); Cassian, Conference 17; the Jewish Encyclopedia ('remarkable women', 'four great beauties', Megillah 15a); Merriam-Webster (Beaumont and Fletcher's Scornful Lady, 1616) and the 1911 Britannica ('handmaid').
Calendar: no Abigail in the OCA's Forefathers page on disk, nor in any calendar file searched; the page says so plainly.
